operations.name: Abijah Adams

expected.name: Abijah Adams
expected.description:
Abijah Adams was the brother of Thomas Adams, editor of the Boston Independent Chronicle, and the bookkeeper at the paper. After Thomas Adams's federal Sedition Act prosecution lapsed when he died in 1799, Massachusetts state authorities prosecuted Abijah for contempt of the Massachusetts General Court (the state legislature) over a Chronicle editorial that had accused the legislature of unconstitutional conduct in passing resolutions condemning Virginia and Kentucky for their opposition to the federal Sedition and Alien Acts.

Tried before Chief Justice Francis Dana of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in February 1799, he was convicted of contempt and sentenced to thirty days in the Boston jail plus \$5 in costs. The case has been described by historians as the only successful state-level common-law prosecution for criticizing a legislature in the Sedition Act period and is regarded as one of the most aggressive uses of judicial contempt against the press in early American history.

updates.description: Abijah Adams was the brother of Thomas Adams, editor of Boston's Independent Chronicle, and worked at the newspaper. Massachusetts authorities prosecuted him under state common law over an editorial criticizing the legislature's condemnation of the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions. He was arrested on February 27, 1799 and released on bail before his March trial before Chief Justice Francis Dana. Convicted of seditious libel, he received thirty days in jail. He was released in April 1799. The prosecution was separate from the federal Sedition Act proceedings against his brother, who died in May 1799.

operations.research_note: Correct biography chronology that placed prosecution after brother's death and trial in February.

operations.name: Edward Sistrunk

expected.name: Edward Sistrunk
expected.description:
Omar Askia Ali was a member of the Nation of Islam who was leading a political campaign to improve conditions in his neighborhood in Philadelphia and remove drugs from the area. Local residents reported that a group of corrupt cops had been robbing addicts and dealers to steal their supply and resell the drugs themselves. While working on this campaign Omar was harassed by police and eventually arrested for a furniture store robbery in which an employee was shot and killed. The head investigator for the robbery Detective William O'Brien had previously threatened Omar to stop his campaign of ending the drug trade and was known in the area as a corrupt cop who would steal and sell drugs. Detective O'Brien was later sentenced to 5 years in prison for bribery and drug dealing. Detective O'Brien claimed he had arrested Omar after a witness identified him as one of the robbers from a photograph of Omar he had shown them. During the trial it was revealed that the witness never identified Omar and instead prosecutors changed their story to claim a police informant told them Omar had committed the robbery. The alleged informant was never allowed to be cross-examined by the defense and Omar was convicted of murder by an all-white jury and sentenced to life in prison.

He died in custody in 2024, at 84, last held at SCI Rockview; the exact date is undocumented. Prison Radio records him as deceased, and he no longer appears in the Pennsylvania Department of Corrections locator.
